The phrase 'non-skeletal deformation' in the claim is likely a slightly imprecise way of saying 'deformation that is not skeletal' (i.e., static) or simply referring to the static mode's lack of skeletal animation. Given the explicit support for static mode and the switching logic, the core facts are supported.

It differs from sibling methods by baking bone weights and group assignments into the voxel structure during offline voxelization, allowing runtime assembly of per-bone chunk components attached to a hidden skeleton, rather than computing skinning or deformation on the GPU during rasterization [S1, unofficial].

The claim accurately reflects the evidence provided in Source [S1]. The evidence states that the system converts a SkeletalMesh to voxel data at editor time (offline voxelization), propagates bone weights and assigns dominant bones to voxels (baking bone weights and group assignments), and at runtime creates a 'HiddenSkeleton' with 'BoneChunks' attached to it (runtime assembly of per-bone chunk components attached to a hidden skeleton). It explicitly contrasts this with GPU skinning by describing the assembly of pre-computed chunks rather than computing deformation on the GPU during rasterization.
